header.title: Exameron: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Ambrose, Saint, Bishop of Milan
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's stoa0022.stoa054.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's CSEL (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0022.stoa054.opp-la: 'You' is the moon, addressed in the preceding sections. [quasi] is bracketed by the editor as an intrusion and not translated. 'nocere non scientiae' is corrupt; the sense is taken as 'cannot harm'. prouidentiam and amori are corrupt; the sense seems to be that Paul punished a magician (Elymas) with blindness. canniuum = carminum.

The section number '9,24' at the start is omitted. 'aut diuersisque adountius' is garbled; read as 'aut diuersi quoque praenuntius', 'or a herald of the opposite'. strauit after excutiatur is a stray word, not translated. 'et sibi excitet' is garbled; rendered by sense ('look to themselves'). sed Chaldaeus is taken as 'or Chaldean'; aeiis = aeris.

nodes.text: How ridiculous, moreover, that people commonly believe that you can be drawn down by magic spells! These are old wives' tales and the opinions of the crowd. For who would suppose that a work of God appointed to so great a service could be assailed by Chaldean superstitions? He who transforms himself into an angel of light may have fallen — and he was brought down by his own will, not by the power of spells. Indeed in this too, O Church, you are thought capable of being drawn down, as it were, from your place and station. Many assail the Church, but the spells of the witch's art [cannot] harm her. Enchanters have no power where the song of Christ is sung every day. She has her own enchanter, the Lord Jesus, through whom she has made void the spells of enchanting magicians and the venoms of serpents; and she herself, like the serpent lifted up, devours snakes; and though the deadly spell of the Egyptians mutter [against her], it is blunted in the name of Christ. So too Paul [punished] the magician not only with the weakness of his witch's art but also with the loss of his eyes. So Peter, when Simon sought the heights of heaven in magic flight, broke the power of his spells and threw him down and laid him low.

The sea urchin — a tiny creature, cheap and contemptible (I mean the marine one) — is often wont to be for sailors an indicator of a coming storm, or a herald of the opposite. In short, when it senses beforehand a gale of winds, it seizes a sturdy pebble and carries it like ballast and drags it like an anchor, so as not to be dislodged. So it does not balance itself by its own strength, but steadies and steers itself by a weight not its own. From this indication sailors take, as it were, a sign of coming disturbance and look to themselves, lest an unforeseen whirlwind find them unprepared. What mathematician, what astrologer, or Chaldean can thus grasp the courses of the stars, thus the movements and signs of the sky? By what ingenuity did it gather these things, from what teacher did it learn them? Who was its interpreter of so great an augury? Men see the turbulence of the air and are often deceived, because often [the sky] dispels it without a storm: the sea urchin is not deceived; its own signs never pass the sea urchin by.
